title: Premium Skincare: +168% GMV Across Three SEA Markets
excerpt: A medical-grade skincare launch grew GMV 168% in three months after customer-journey analysis rerouted it from D2C to marketplaces. Read the case.
rm_desc: Skincare marketplace launch: GMV grew 168% after rerouting from D2C to Shopee and Lazada. Read the case.
content: This skincare marketplace launch covers a premium medical-grade brand entering three Southeast Asian markets at once, on under 0.5% share of category spend. The launch plan assumed a D2C site because the brand sold that way at home.

Customer-journey analysis across the three launch markets came before any spend was committed, and it rerouted the launch from the planned D2C site to Shopee and Lazada, where the category in those markets actually buys. Content was built for the marketplace environment rather than ported from the brand site, with weekly creative rotation letting the data pick winners.

A separate doctor-and-dermatologist B2B strategy ran in Singapore, because the buyer there differs from the consumer buyer everywhere else in the launch. Getting the channel right before spending on it is most of what a marketplace launch actually is; the media plan itself is the comparatively easy part once the underlying routing decision has already been made correctly.
Why marketplaces over the brand's own site

The category decided this, not a template preference. In several Southeast Asian skincare markets, marketplaces like Shopee carry the trust signals a new entrant has not built yet, reviews, seller ratings, buyer protection, that a brand-new D2C domain cannot replicate in month one. A skincare marketplace launch that insists on driving traffic to an unproven domain is paying a trust tax the marketplace has already resolved for its buyers. That does not hold everywhere; it held here, and the customer-journey data is what confirmed it before the budget committed rather than after the first disappointing month of traffic.

GMV grew 168% through Shopee and Lazada in the first three months of the skincare marketplace launch, with 65,000 new visitors averaging 2 minutes 20 seconds with the content, all of it achieved on under 0.5% of total category spend in the region.

The number belongs to the routing decision. The customer-journey data disagreed with the launch plan, and the plan changed, that is the whole case. The lesson generalises; the playbook does not: the same engagement ran a clinical B2B strategy in Singapore because the channel follows the buyer, and buyers differ by market. A skincare marketplace launch in a different category, or a different pair of countries, would need its own customer-journey analysis before assuming the same routing applies.
What we would check before repeating this

Two things this case does not prove on its own: that marketplaces always beat a D2C site, and that 168% is a repeatable baseline. Both depend heavily on category dynamics and starting market share, and a skincare marketplace launch attempted in a more saturated category with several strong incumbents already established would very likely see a meaningfully different number even with the identical routing logic applied correctly and carefully. What generalises is the method: checking where the category actually buys before building the launch plan around an assumption inherited from a different, home market. That check costs a few weeks of analysis and saves months of a launch built on the wrong channel.

This engagement combined social and creator distribution with the marketplace strategy above; the full service scope is on our services page. Brands weighing a similar skincare marketplace launch into Singapore, Malaysia or the wider region can start there before scoping a market-entry engagement of their own.
Client described rather than named, and all figures are reported exactly as recorded at the time.
